Ferritin—an acute-phase reactant and marker of iron storage—reflects chronic inflammation, which is known to be involved in CKD pathogenesis [ 41 , 42 ].

To better determine whether ferritin can reliably predict CKD risk, it is crucial to conduct detailed studies with multiple ferritin measurements, as well as information on acute infection and hemoglobin over time in relation to eGFR and albuminuria, and in multiple ethnic groups.
69.Rationale: This option overstates the implications of the null CRP result. The authors do not conclude that chronic inflammation is not a driver of CKD; rather, they propose explanations (e.g., inflammatory adaptation) for why CRP may not have shown an association in this setting. They treat ferritin as a stronger predictor and as reflecting chronic inflammation, but they caution that ferritin is nonspecific and that repeated measures and additional data are needed to clarify mechanisms. Thus it is incorrect to conclude definitively that chronic inflammation is not a driver and that ferritin is unequivocally the superior inflammation marker based solely on the observed CRP null result.

young or middle-aged individuals are more likely to engage in occupational and outdoor activities that could increase the possibility for exposure to extreme temperatures [ 31–35 ].

economically disadvantaged males tend to work in relatively more intensive industries (such as construction, agriculture, and transportation) that can increase exposure to outdoor extreme temperatures, compared with females and males who are not socially marginalized [ 6 ].

we observed a positive association between ED admissions for substance abuse disorders and cold temperatures among MA-eligible patients in contrast to the negative association that was observed in the non-eligible group ( Supplementary Table S8 ; see online supplementary material for a color version of this table).
we cautiously conjectured that these results might have been related to occupational and outdoor activities in young and middle-aged populations.

we cautiously conjectured that these results might have been related to occupational and outdoor activities in young and middle-aged populations.

71.Option: Adjust for central adiposity as a covariate in a Cox proportional hazards model to estimate the association between age at menarche and diabetes incidence
Evidence: The final set of models incorporated adiposity measures as potential mediating factors: waist circumference as a measure of central obesity (model 4a) and BMI as a measure of general obesity (model 4b).

We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age.
71.Rationale: While adjusting for central adiposity in a Cox model is an appropriate way to control for confounding or to estimate the direct association, it does not evaluate whether the risk differs across levels of central adiposity (effect modification). The passage indicates the authors both adjusted for adiposity (models 4a/4b) and separately tested for interaction and stratified by obesity. To assess whether the association differs by central adiposity, adjustment alone is insufficient—an interaction test or stratified analysis is required.

71.Option: Test for interaction between age at menarche and central adiposity using a Cox proportional hazards model with an interaction term, and report stratified hazard ratios
Evidence: We assessed statistical interaction between age at menarche and obesity (BMI and waist circumference classifications, separately) using the P -value of the Wald test and also conducted Cox proportional hazards analyses stratified by obesity classification.
We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age.
71.Rationale: The question asks how to evaluate whether diabetes risk differs by menarche age among women with varying central adiposity. The appropriate approach for effect modification in a prospective cohort analyzed with time-to-event methods is to include an interaction term between age at menarche and central adiposity in a Cox model, test the interaction (e.g., Wald test), and present stratified hazard ratios. The passage explicitly describes performing this exact procedure, supporting that this is the most appropriate method.

71.Option: Use a mediation analysis to assess whether the effect of age at menarche on diabetes is transmitted through central adiposity
Evidence: The final set of models incorporated adiposity measures as potential mediating factors: waist circumference as a measure of central obesity (model 4a) and BMI as a measure of general obesity (model 4b).
many of these factors are likely mediators which ought not to be adjusted for to derive unconfounded associations.
71.Rationale: Mediation analysis addresses whether central adiposity lies on the causal pathway between menarche age and diabetes (i.e., transmission of effect), not whether the association differs across levels of adiposity (effect modification). The question specifically asks about differences in risk by adiposity level, so mediation is not the correct analytic approach. The passage acknowledges adiposity as a potential mediator, but that is a different research question from testing effect modification.

71.Option: Match cases and controls on central adiposity status to reduce confounding in a case-control analysis of age at menarche and diabetes
Evidence: The CARRS study was established in 2010–12 as a multi-centric, community-based prospective study to identify risk factors for cardio-metabolic diseases among South Asians.
We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age.
71.Rationale: Matching cases and controls is a technique for case-control studies. This analysis is a prospective cohort with time-to-event (Cox) analysis; there are no matched case-control samples described. Moreover, matching on central adiposity would preclude assessing whether the association differs by adiposity (it would remove variation in the matching variable). Therefore, matching cases and controls on central adiposity is inappropriate here.

72.Option: Enables identification of specific age windows when exposure has the greatest impact on adult outcomes by modeling continuous, time-varying effects while accounting for correlated pollutants
Evidence: To explore susceptible windows, we fitted log Poisson DLMs with robust standard error estimators with a cross-basis of a log-linear exposure–response association based on prior work [ 18 ] and a lag–response association using a natural cubic spline smooth function.
